utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As I indicated yesterday, the Chamber wants to deliver, at least partly deliver, the decision on the motion in limine under the Rule 73 motion as filed by the Gotovina Defence. This is the Chamber's decision on part of Gotovina Defence's Rule 73 motion in limine. On the 6th of March 2008, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion requesting the Chamber to issue an order precluding the Prosecution from introducing testimony through a proposed Prosecution expert witness on whether targets selected and hit during Operation Storm were legitimate military targets. The Gotovina Defence also requested the Chamber to issue an order precluding the Prosecution from, and I quote, "Claiming that the Prosecution's fact witnesses are experts in artillery and thereby competent to tell the Trial Chamber whether particular targets were civilian or military." The Markac Defence joined the motion on the 25th of March. The Prosecution responded on the 20th of March, asking the Chamber to dismiss the motion. The Gotovina Defence requested leave to reply, and the Chamber denied this request yesterday on the 21st of April. The Chamber will deal with the first request in the motion at a later stage. As for the second request, one of the witnesses concerned is today's witness, Andrew Leslie. The determination of whether a specific target is civilian or military is ultimately one to be made by the Chamber. The Chamber considers that there is no need for an order preventing the Prosecution from describing their witnesses in any particular way, nor is there a need for an order preventing the Prosecution from eliciting opinions from fact witnesses. That said, the Chamber reminds both parties that it is best assisted by a fact witness when that witness describes what he or she has personally observed, although certain testimonies do not always allow for a clear distinction between facts and conclusions. If the testimony of a witness contains opinions or conclusions, the Chamber would expect the parties to explore the factual basis of the opinion or the conclusion. That would also be the proper time for the Defence to raise the matters brought up in the motion. In this respect, the Chamber is aware that witnesses have different backgrounds and different professional experiences which enable them to observe, understand, and interpret observations in different ways. Accordingly, the Chamber rejects the second request in the Gotovina Defence motion. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness which, as I understand, is Mr. Andrew Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Leslie. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is already in your hands. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Mr. Leslie, you may be a bit surprised that I address you as "Mr. Leslie." That is not a sign of disrespect for your functions, not in any way. This Chamber usually addresses whomever comes before this Chamber in their personal capacity, and that's the only reason why I call you "Mr. Leslie" where others may choose to do it in a different way. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, can we begin simply by having you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: My name is Andrew Brook Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what is your current profession and position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I am a professional soldier in the Canadian Armed Forces. My current position is the Chief of Land Staff or the Commander of Canada's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your current rank?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I'm a Lieutenant-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, I'd like to ask you relatively quickly some questions about your background. I'll attempt to do so by moving through it as quickly as I can and asking you to confirm the information I understand to be accurate, if, indeed, it is correct. First of all, is it correct that you have been in the military since 1977 when you joined the army reserves as an artilleryman?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while studying in England during that time, you were attached to the Honourable Artillery Company?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in 1981, you transferred to the regular force and remained as an artilleryman?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you served as battery commander of artillery?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that eventually, you commanded the 1st Regiment Royal Canadian Horse Artillery?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've attended various advanced courses in artillery and participated in numerous international exercises involving various weapons systems?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those involved weapons systems from varied countries such as Germany, France, Britain, Norway, The Netherlands, and other countries?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you -- that your entire career, up to the point of your service in the Krajina in 1995, was in the artillery?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I served as a gunner or as an artillery officer. There were two occasions, each of two years duration in the years leading up to my service in the Krajina, where I was employed as a staff officer. So I was not specifically serving the guns. I was employed as a staff officer in a variety of headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Leslie. The interpreters sometimes have the advantage of two people speaking in different languages. Here, however, you are speaking the same language; and, therefore, you're invited to make a short break before answering the question, just as Mr. Tieger is invited not to ask his question until after a short pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That, of course, applies equally as the Court noted, to counsel, and to questions posed either by the Court or by other counsel. So we'll all try to be attentive to the translation issues. General Leslie, I'll return shortly to your deployment to the Krajina in 1995, but I wanted to complete quickly questions about your background. Is it correct that, in 1997, you served as the commander of the 1st Canadian Mechanised Brigade group and infantry or heavy combat formation group where the focus was on live fire combined arms training?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you then become in 2000 the commander of the communications brigade responsible for commanding communications field groups and regiments?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: A minor correction. It was not a brigade per se, it was a formation of brigade size, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 2002, did you become commander of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I'm sorry about the speed to all those who are interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 2002, General Leslie, did you become commander of land force central area responsible for four brigades?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in 2003, did you become commander of the land forces in Kabul; that is, commander of joint and combined international forces, the majority of whom were Canadian?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was the commander of Joint Task Force Kabul, and my second hat was as deputy commander of the International Security Assistance Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in 2004, did you become deputy commander of the Canadian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you study as a full time Ph.D. student for a time after that at the Royal Military College?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 2005, did you become Director General of strategic planning for the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: For the armed forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in 2006, did you become commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated earlier that I would be returning shortly to your service in the Krajina in 1995. When were you deployed to the Krajina and to what part?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was deployed on the 1st of March, 1995, and my position was as Chief of Staff Sector South located in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, General Leslie, and that was -- I'm sorry. Let me ask you: Chief of Staff Sector South for what organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: For the United Nations protection force as part of the UNCRO command, as part of Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in general, who was UNCRO's task or responsibilities in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: UNCRO's task was to implement the will of the United Nations Security Council as stated in a variety of resolutions. In essence, it was to maintain the zone of separation, to provide surveillance and observation on the zone of separation, to ensure that none of the warring factions entered the zone of separation, and to assist the Secretary General or the special representative of the Secretary General in the accomplishment of his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with the objective of ensuring the warring factions did not penetrate the zone of separation on to the other side, was UNCRO equipped to prevent all incursions irrespective of size?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, it was not. The UNCRO forces were equipped mainly for self-defence purposes. There were very little, if any, what we would consider heavy weapons such as tanks, medium artillery, heavy artillery. The main table of organisation and equipment for the battalions in Sector South was much akin to that of light infantry battalions, and most of their expertise was focused on observation, surveillance, and patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just for clarification, although I think it's clear, on what side of the zone of separation was UNCRO Sector South located?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The troops that comprised the Sector South formation were located on the side of the rebel Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your duties or responsibilities as Chief of Staff for Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, I was directly responsible to my commander who, when I first arrived, was Major-General Kutil from the Czech Republic and, later, Brigadier General Forand from Canada. As Chief of Staff, I was responsible to my commander for the efficient functioning and integration of the various staff branches that made up Sector South headquarters. And on his behalf, I would assist in the day-to-day running of the sector, supervise the staff activities within Sector South headquarters, and to him I was also responsible for the layout, the security, and the efficient administration of all the elements that were located in the Sector South compound. On top of that, I would be assigned whatever duties the commander felt appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly the composition of UNCRO in Sector South and where UNCRO units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Headquarters Sector South was located on the southern edge of the city or town of Knin. The field troops consisted of four line battalions. To the north, we had the Czech battalion; to the north centre, we had the Jordanian battalion; in the south centre, we had the Canadian battalion; and, in the south, we had the Kenyan battalion. On the left, the zone of separation was anchored to the Dinara mountains; and on the right, it extended all the way up through the mountain range of the Velebits and beyond. Furthermore, we had a variety of support units which consisted of a Czech medical company and a surgical hospital section which was located with Sector South headquarters. We had a military police company, which was international in composition, located in Sector South headquarters. We had attached to us an Indonesian engineer organisation of about company size, and as well we had a Slovak engineer company which was busy throughout the sector. There were some minor staff branches, specialist activities, both composed of great folk from the United Nations civil service, contractual employees, local employees, most of whom were located in and around Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, to summarize, the headquarters of Sector South was located in Knin, and the -- a number of the units you've described were located in -- outside of Knin in various parts of Sector South as you've described.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, is it correct, General Leslie, that you remained as Chief of Staff of Sector South until approximately the 9th of August when you became Chief of Staff for UNCRO in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions, then, about Knin immediately before the commencement of Operation Storm on the 4th of August. First of all, General, did you live in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the town? Did you walk around it or engage in recreational activity around it? Did you become familiar with the town?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was relatively familiar with the town. I lived in the top floor of a two-storey building downtown. I would habitually walk to work in the morning; and if it wasn't dark by the time I finished work, I would often walk home. As well, when the opportunity presented itself, I would engage in physical fitness activity and training, running, in and around the town itself. So I was relatively familiar with the town, considering I lived there for five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you quickly about the demographics of the town. Had the size of the population of Knin changed in the period shortly preceding Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: When I first arrived in Knin in March, and these are only estimates and not meant to sound as if they're definitive numbers, but the population of Knin was probably somewhere in the order of 20.000 to 25.000. As tensions mounted, and it became fairly obvious that imminent hostilities were looming, the population of Knin had swollen to somewhere around 35.000 in the days immediately preceding the events of the 4th and 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who -- where had the people who had increased the size of Knin come from? Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: In the main, I believe they were the families of those who were concerned that their villages and towns were close to the zone or closer to the zone of separation and, therefore, had a higher probability of risk. So the town, immediately prior to the 4th and 5th of August, was populated by mainly the elderly, women, and children, as the vast majority of fighting-aged males had been essentially mobilised and deployed into the zone of separation in a variety of defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you describe the extent of the military presence in Knin in the period preceding Operation Storm, soldiers or fixed positions or other aspects of the military presence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I would like to break that period down into two. Roughly between March and May, Knin was a transit point and a collection point for the fighting aged males who were to be seen in many, many parts of Knin. The unemployment rate was very high, so it was very common to see large numbers of soldiers or militia in and around Knin. From about mid-May onwards that was no longer the case because the soldiers had been deployed or the militia had been deployed into the zone of separation. The military presence in Knin in the period immediately prior to the 4th and 5th of August, so the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, was minimal in the sense that anybody who could fight had been deployed into the zone of separation, though there were the occasional staff to be seen and there was the occasional uniform to be seen in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did soldiers come periodically to visit their families or visit Knin for -- on R & R, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the period prior to the end of July and very early August, the -- that was often the case where small groups of soldiers or militiamen could be seen down near the train yards waiting for the buses to take them back to what they considered the front, but all this sort of activity and movement stopped as of roughly the 1st of August as the vast majority of fighting-aged males had been deployed into the zone of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were you able to observe about military preparations immediately prior to Storm in Knin itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The defensive preparations in and around Knin were essentially non-existent. There were extensive defensive preparations done by the Serbs on their side of the zone of separation; but in terms of the town itself, none of the routes were prepared for demolitions. There was no construction of fortifications or bunkers. Glass was not taken out of the windows. The windows were not taped to mitigate against splinter damage. There were no shells or trenches being constructed. There were no berms to canalise attacking forces. There were none of those routine defensive preparations that one would expect for what could potentially be a major combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you've described the increase in the size of the civilian population in Knin in the period preceding Operation Storm. Did you observe whether any of the population of Knin had left the area in the days immediately preceding Storm, that is, immediately before August 4th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: There were some elements of the local population that had left in roughly the week prior to the 4th and 5th of August. How many, I don't know. It did not appear to make a sizeable reduction in the mass of people that I would see in and around the streets of Knin. We were aware anecdotally that a variety of Serbian refugees or Serbs from Knin had tried to get across the border into the Serb-controlled areas of Bosnia but had been turned around and sent back to Knin. But this is anecdote; it is not based on observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, how and when did you first learn that Operation Storm would take place or would commence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The first confirmed indication we had was at roughly 20 minutes after 3.00 on the 4th of August when the Sector South headquarters received an indication from UNCRO headquarters, our superior headquarters in Zagreb, that an attack by the Croatian Forces to recapture the Krajina was imminent. Over the course of the subsequent hours, there were many such reports from different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what steps were taken by UNCRO staff in response to that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that, sir. I wasn't at UNCRO headquarters at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise for that question. What steps were taken at Sector South headquarters in response to that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The commander and his command team were immediately advised, and it was decided to implement the emergency recall plan, whose aim was to get all our people who were currently living outside of the compound back into the compound and from there into the bunkers. That process took several hours. At some point, and I can't remember the exact time without referring to my notes, the recall emergency sirens were activated which were very loud and could be heard throughout most of Knin as an audible cue for those people that we couldn't contact by either telephone or radio to get themselves back to Sector South headquarters immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, what was your role during this process? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: My main role was in shepherding people into the bunkers and making sure that, as officers and soldiers came in, they were allocated to tasks. The reason why this was especially complicated is, in the normal functioning of Sector South headquarters, a variety of the staff branches had routine administrative work to be done. Of course, that routine administrative work was no longer important, so people were either in the bunkers or allocated to local security tasks or assisting in staffing the operations centre where General Forand and his operations staff had the duty to run the entirety of the sector. So, in essence, my job was to take care of everything that wasn't in the operations centre, and to ensure that the commander was free to focus on running his sector, with the main focus being protection of our personnel and making sure the various steps were initiated to recall our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall when the -- when Operation Storm began, when the attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I recall that at approximately 5.02 on the morning of the 4th of August, a massive artillery barrage impacted in and around Knin; and to my mind, that was the commencement of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you say "massive artillery barrage." Can you describe the nature or intensity of that barrage for the Court?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The number of detonations which was almost simultaneous indicated that whatever indirect fire systems had been used had obviously been told to fire at a specific moment in time. There were a multiplicity of explosions into one continuous roar that lasted for a minute or two followed by a pause of a minute or two, and then the cycle repeated itself with the synchronicity of the explosions starting to become mixed. To explain after the first couple of minutes instead of sort of a continuous roar and a pause and another roar, it turned into consistent shell fire .

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say consistent shell fire after describing the rough timing that you did. Can you also give the Court any indication of the relative intensity of that consistent shell fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I would say the intensity was high between roughly 5.00 in the morning of the 4th until approximately 7.00 in terms of the total number of explosions, though there would be variances between when those explosions occurred. So, in the first initial salvo, all the explosions occurred almost at the same time. As the first hour or two wore on, there were the same relative number of explosions over time, but it wasn't as controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that, at approximately 7.00, there was a change in the intensity of the shell fire. Can you describe for the Court the nature of the change that occurred after approximately the first of couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: At approximately 7.00, or around approximately 7.00, the fire diminished markedly; and instead of having explosions all over the city of a consistent nature, the explosions and shell fire was grouped across specific regions of the city which varied, wherein you'd have a shell detonating, a minute or two or three would go by, another shell detonating 200 to 300 metres away from where the first one went off. That process would be repeated several times. Then you'd have four, five, or six shells landing fairly tightly grouped together. This process would be repeated essentially throughout most of the day at a lessened intensity as compared to what happened between 5.00 and 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this process you've just described, with a shell and then another shell and then a group of shells, were you familiar with that process; and if so, can you tell us its significance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I am familiar with the process. And in my opinion, the significance is that after the additional -- the original opening barrage, which appeared to be random and relatively evenly distributed across the entirety of the town, the Croatian gunners were then engaging in what is known as target grid procedure, wherein a battery of guns, which can be two, three, four, five, six guns grouped together, would be adjusted by visual observation on to a specific target. The process is one gun fires of that grouping; the visual observation correction is then made to move that shell; corrections are then computed and passed to the other guns; another round is fired from the original gun to adjust that specifically on to where your target might lie. Then once the observer is relatively satisfied that his one gun is in the target area, because artillery is an area weapons system, or certainly was in those days, then all the guns of the battery would be fired at that single point; and therein you'd have three, four, five, or six detonations in relatively close proximity both in time and space. It's a process I've seen hundreds of times in a variety of training exercises in Canada and other artillery ranges throughout NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's the process of directing the weaponry toward a particular target?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about your whereabouts during the course of August 4th and what you observed during that time. First of all, let me ask you, with respect to the -- starting at during the time when efforts were being made to get personnel to safety shortly before and shortly after the attack commenced, what were you doing, where were you, and what were you able to observe?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: By 3.30, I -- 3.30 in the morning on the 4th of August, I was in my office. I don't think I returned to my office until around 6.00, though I can't be sure. The vast majority of time between 3.30 and, say, 5.30 was spent making sure people were organised to move towards the appropriate bunkers, to populate the operations centres with people as they became available, to make sure that the Sector South security staff had started the process of dispatching vehicles to pick people up, and to try and control the rather frenzied activity of people coming in to the camp from their residences in and around Knin, realising that such-and-such and so-and-so had not made it in yet and trying to go back out and pick them up, which was a relatively complicated process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of what you've described as the initial intense barrage in the first couple of hours of the attack, were you able to see from any of the positions that you were in where shells landing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: From the moment of the initial barrage until approximately 6.00, I do not recall having any time to actually watch where the shell fire was landing. It was dark, and there were many other issues which prevented me from doing so. At around 6.00, not precisely, I joined several others in -- on a balcony just opposite my office on, I believe, the 3rd floor of Sector South headquarters for a period of time, not long, and was able to observe the artillery fire, which as of around 6.00 had no discernible pattern, and it was unknown to any of us as to what targets were actually being engaged because of the random nature of the distribution of fire. So I would - pardon my long-windedness - I would say that the first time I was able to actually observe the fire was for a brief period at approximately 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What area of Knin were you able to observe during the first couple of hours, during the time you described observing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sector South headquarters is located on the southern edge of Knin, and my balcony was facing north. I would say that in terms of direct observation, you could see somewhere close to 1500 metres before the first row of buildings became evident, and then you could see larger buildings in the foreground and middle ground. The view was blocked on the left by the castle and on the right by a small knoll or terrain feature. I would say the observation over the southern third of the city in terms of looking at the roof tops and the larger structures was quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that the artillery fire which you observed had no discernible pattern. Did you see any efforts to correct fire in the manner you described before; that is, so that particular targets could be hit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the shell fire that you observed, although I understand you described it earlier as being spread out over a wide area, was it grouped in any particular part of Knin, either the downtown area, outside area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: In the main --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I hate to interrupt, Judge, but I do believe the witness said he couldn't see most of the areas that we're describing. I mean, if he's talking about a specific area that the witness observed, that will be fine; but I just take that with the caveat of what the witness just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he described clearly in what respect his view was limited. Then I take it that Mr. Tieger's questions are now about that what he could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you can answer the question. Do you need me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't. Thank you. I have it here. The -- when observing shell fire, and this was the case in Knin, I'd like to point out, if I may, that it was a very rare occasion when we, in Sector South, actually saw a round detonate on the ground. The rounds would be falling in and amongst the buildings, and what you would see breaking the roof line was the ball of grey dust, smoke, and debris being thrown up by the force of the explosion. So, although, for example, we may have had excellent visibility out to 1.000, 2.000, in certain cases more metres, you could see where shells were landing in terms of a rough area by the fact that the debris cloud of grey smoke would break the roof line. So, in that context, the majority of the shells appeared to be grouped in what I will call the centre of the town, but there was fire at that time essentially all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, after the -- I asked you earlier about the first couple of hours of the attack during which you had earlier described the barrage that took place. After the first couple of hours, did you have the opportunity to observe the shelling that was taking place; and, if so, from what position or positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: From about 7.00 onwards, the day was almost a constant cycle of moving between the bunkers, the front gate, the perimeter of the compound, up to the Czech medical facility just below the helipad, back to the OP centre to check in; and then the cycle was repeated almost continuously. There were no staff branches or activities for me to coordinate, and General Forand, quite properly, was in the operations centre running his sector. So most of my day was spent outside, and a significant portion of that period was spent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, there might be some confusion as to the question. The last line of the question was, "and if so, from what position or positions?" Now, Mr. Tieger, I do not know whether you had in mind from what position or positions the witness observed or from what position or what positions the shelling took place. I got the impression that you had the latter in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour, for that opportunity to clarify. My question was about the opportunity to see the shelling that was taking place; and if so, where the witness was when he observed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I was listening with a wrong ear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, sir, I would say it varied between my office window -- sorry, my office balcony which was actually, to be accurate, on the opposite side of the hallway from my office facing towards the town; and at other vantage points inside Sector South compound, probably the best position of observation was in the area at the helipad, which is the highest point in the Sector South compound headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me then turn to the question that the Presiding Judge thought I was asking at the time. Where did you observe the shelling taking place; that is, where were the shells landing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Between 6.00 and 7.00, sir, I cannot precisely specify where the centre of mass of shells was landing because as mentioned, it was, from what I could see, all over the place. From about 7.00 onwards, it was much easier to define. The mass of shells were landing on mainly residential areas grouped in the centre of town, but that did not mean that the smaller groupings of buildings on the outskirts were immune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier, you described the observational range of what you could see from the balcony. Were you able to see more or less of the town from the other positions in the compound during the course of the day when you were making the observations you just described?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: As you walked up the hill from Sector South headquarters, past the kitchen facilities and in the area of the Czech hospital unit, you could see much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask Mr. Registrar to call up 65 ter number 403.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you should see, on a screen in front of you, 65 ter number 403, a document which is an UNCRO document. At the top, we see and headed, "Protest attacks on innocent civilians and UN installations," and it's signed by General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, General Leslie?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you aware of this document on August 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that such a document was going to be prepared or sent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I believe it was at some time prior to noon. I honestly can't recall at what point during that rather frenzied series of activities the document itself was crafted. To the best of my recollection, it was crafted by an officer, an excellent officer called Lieutenant-Colonel Shaun Tymchuk; and it was based on the reports that had been given to the area commander in his operations centre from his various battalions on the line and also from what he himself could see and comment on vis-a-vis Knin. So I believe it first originated some time prior to noon on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, were you contacted about the intention to send this or consulted in connection with the anticipation of preparing and sending this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was aware of it. I think the idea originated with General Forand, and I had very little input into its content. I did not -- I cannot claim any credit for writing it. I was aware that it was being sent; however, it was being sent out of the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you understand the purpose of this document to be?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: To achieve an immediate cessation of the indirect fire artillery attacks on not only Knin but the other towns mentioned, and to also secure an immediate withdrawal of the combatant forces from the zone of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was this protest letter to be provided -- well, first of all, to whom was the letter sent or the protest letter sent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The process letter was sent by the operations centre and also by the senior liaison officer. The traditional route - and I believe that's the route that occurred with this document, though, once again, I wish to point out I was not in the operations centre - was via the Croatian army liaison officer who was responsible for interactions between General Gotovina's organisation and Sector South, and this individual was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologize, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, I think we're in the area, Judge, based on his initial answer, and I would think Your Honour was talking to the witness about what he knew and what he observed. Quite clearly, from his answer, he does not know what happened to this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps you might explore where the witness said, "and I believe that's the route that occurred with this document," what factual knowledge is available and what's the source of this knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I was, in fact, going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, you've indicated the traditional route for communicating such a document to the Croatian army. In this particular case, can you tell us what you know about what happened with this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was also communicated to UNCRO headquarters, UNPF headquarters, it was distributed to the CIVPOL organisation, the UNMO organisation, all with a view to ensuring that it made its way as expeditiously as possible to the appropriate Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you have any information about whether the document was received by Croatian army authorities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I'm told that it was, but I have no personal knowledge of its receipt by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I may have jumped a step; and that is, in connection with what you described as the traditional route to get such documents to Croatian army authorities, to General Gotovina, or other persons to whom such documents were directed, can you describe what that traditional route was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, the traditional route was twofold. One was via the senior liaison officer to Captain of Marine Lukovic, dealing specifically with General Gotovina's fighting formations. Also, at the same time, a copy would be sent via the United Nations Military Observer organisation to their liaison officer who was also with the Croatian army liaison team. The third traditional route was via UNCRO headquarters where, when such documents were sent or received, they were then taken across to the senior Croatian army liaison officer, a gentleman by the name of General Plestina, I believe his name was, who essentially replicated the functions of Captain of Marine Lukovic but one level higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, one of the previous answers of the witness was, "I'm told that it was, but I have no personal knowledge of its receipt by the Croatian authorities." Could you tell us who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the big concerns that General Forand had that afternoon and evening was making sure that the protest letter was widely distributed; and so I believe, though I cannot state with certainty, sir, that Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk informed that OPs update conference in the evening of the 5th -- no, the 4th, that the letter had been sent to the UNMOs and had been sent to the KLO staff, the Croatian Army Liaison Officer staff, headed by Captain of Marine Lukovic. Colonel Norris Pettis, who is the Chief of Staff UNCRO, also confirmed to me that a copy had been sent to General Plestina that evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question, of course, was primarily concerned not on sending but on receiving. Could you tell us whether he also informed you about the letter not only being sent but also delivered or receipt confirmed or more information about the receiving side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I can cannot recall such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you cannot recall, then please tell us such. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned a Croatian army officer named Lukovic, Captain of Marine. Did you know him, and did you ever speak with him about this protest letter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Captain Lukovic, very kindly, drove me out of Knin on the 9th of August, and we had an opportunity to exchange a variety of ideas. He was well aware of the letter; but to be absolutely precise, I cannot recall discussing with him whether or not he received it or whether or not he acknowledged receiving it on the 4th of August. He was certainly aware of the letter. He was aware of its contents, aware of its significance. He had seen it, but I cannot recall him saying: I saw this letter at such-and-such a time, at such-and-such a place, on such-and-such a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the context in which the discussion about the letter took place? In other words, were you talking about such letters generally? Were you talking about this letter? Were you talking about the fact that it had been sent on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot remember the trigger or the context of the conversation. I knew him well enough to speak frankly to him. We shared a passion for boats. He was not a friend, but I -- we knew each other well enough to speak frankly. I cannot recall the context in which this letter was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me return to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you leaving the letter at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's all yours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered, just trying to, first of all, on our screen, we see not the whole of the letter at this moment, because the lower part gives some information about telefax exchange, apparently. I do not know how it is translated in B/C/S. I see some handwriting before "August," and this is off some letters I'm not able to decipher or it stands for "04." Now, I wonder what "necitko" means in the translation. Is that illegible; if so, are we then supposed to consider the "04", or whatever it may be, also as illegible? This is not a real translation issue, but rather a legibility issue which perhaps we could -- I don't know whether there is a common understanding of the parties about what is handwritten before "August." At least those who are consulting the translation certainly will not understand that it could possibly be interpreted as "04," because it's presented to them as illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to dispute the translation of "necitko." I can't really see a basis for any ambiguity about what's written there, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement between the parties whether the handwritten portion - where I think there would not be a lot of dispute - is about "04"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there is many disputes about "04" which we will explore thoroughly; however, Judge, I do ask Your Honour to scroll down and read the fax line at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's totally different. That's the 12th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course, that may have triggered my curiosity in this respect. Yes. You see I don't have to even consult it. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, one more question before we leave this document. There are a number of towns listed in the first sentence other than Knin; that is, Drnis, Medak, and others. Do you know whether this was an exhaustive list of the towns about which General Forand and other senior members of Sector South headquarters had information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir. The intent was not for this list to be exhaustive. It was meant to be representative; and the urgency of getting the document out, with an attempt to stop the artillery fire and to get the Croats to withdraw from the zone of separation, was such that it was felt best to send this document as is. That was part of the discussions that took place when the idea of the document originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be leaving the document at this moment. Perhaps that can be - I don't know how the Court wishes to handle it - but I, otherwise, ask that it be marked and tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is an objection to this. I mean, the position on this letter -- there's no evidence this letter was ever received by General Gotovina. An exact duplicate of this letter was sent to another sector to General Norac, which, in fact, General Norac did, in fact, receive, but there is no such documentation reflecting that this letter went to General Gotovina at any time. I will get into it at cross, Judge, and explore those issues with Your Honour; and at this point, I just ask Your Honour to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this an admissibility issue or is it probative value and weight to be given to it? I mean, the witness has testified about this letter; and although he tells us that he has no personal knowledge of the way in which it was delivered and to whom it was delivered exactly, at the same time he speaks about other people in a conversation to be aware of this letter. So, to that extent, it comes to my mind that it's rather weight than admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I just briefly may comment, Judge, and I understand Your Honour's inclination in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If someone writes a letter and there's no foundation that that letter is received by the recipient, then it is not of any probative value. Clearly, the Prosecution has not established, and they could have established by bringing some of these other people in, that this letter was, in fact, received by General Gotovina. With that caveat, it -- I submit to Your Honour that there is no probative value to this letter at this juncture because there is absolutely no evidence from this witness or the Prosecution that the recipient received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that the letter will be admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P83, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P83 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, you've referred, in connection with that letter, to reports that Sector South headquarters was receiving from UNCRO units throughout the sector. Can you just describe generally what information, to the extent you haven't already done so, Sector South was obtaining during the course of the day from the UNCRO units deployed throughout Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. All four line battalions that were in the zone of separation reported, more or less, a certain degree of consistency in the events that happened on the 4th, starting with artillery fires on Serbian Defence positions in the zone of separation, artillery fires on Serbian artillery positions and troops concentrations just behind the zone of separation, artillery fires on large numbers of residential communities within range of the zone of separation, and then Croatian army forces advancing into the zone of separation and, in certain cases, occupying, capturing, disarming of United Nations personnel and seizing of their facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, did you travel outside the Sector South headquarters compound on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court on how many occasions and what the nature of that travel was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: A couple times mounted; a couple of times dismounted. The mounted were sometime shortly after 6.00 for a very short duration where, in the controlled chaos, that was the front gate. There were some issues with UN CIVPOL who were not necessarily on the same recall list as the Sector South United Nations civil staff, and there was a demand for someone who knew where a street was close to the train yard. So I hopped aboard that vehicle, the duration of the trip was about 15 minutes, nothing significant to report. Picked up three people, none of them UN CIVPOL, and came back. The second trip was at some point during the day. There was some bodies outside to the right, and some people were interested in investigating them and putting them in bags. So I just went outside to put a stop to that. Then that evening, I went to the Serbian army liaison detachment to discuss some issues. To the best of my recollection, those were my sojourns outside of Sector South compound on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Serbian army liaison detachment, where was that located? Where was the building or structure where that was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I call it the RSK headquarters, which is not the same as the Ministry of Defence. So it's on the main street, or you get to it via going to the main street before you get to a traffic circle, well before. It's on the left-hand side offset by about 50 metres, and -- well, there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And what did you observe when you got to the RSK headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The building I call the RSK headquarters was damaged. It had some shell fragmentation. It was in the evening of the 4th, and there was a dead body, with some fatigue bottom halves, just tucked away in the approach as you go up the steps. It was essentially deserted by the time I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know when the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I first would like to ask the usher to escort Mr. Leslie out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, and we'll resume in approximately 25 minutes, Mr. Leslie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for scheduling purposes, I think this witness was initially indicated for six and a half hours viva voce which, from what I understood, is not your estimate at this moment anymore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I've attempted to stay in close contact both with court personnel and the Defence in connection with the timing. I certainly anticipate finishing in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This would mean that it's three hours. Then we discussed before this trial started one-to-one ratio Prosecution and Defence teams. Since almost all of the evidence until now was presented under Rule 92 ter, we could not follow that suggestion. It's also not my suggestion that we would follow a one-to-one ratio in relation to this witness, which appears to be a very important witness for the Prosecution and for the Defence as well. Nevertheless, I'd like to know whether the Defence considers it possible, if Mr. Tieger would finish today after approximately three hours, whether we could finish this witness by Thursday. That is a little bit more than two days, that would be a ratio of approximately two-and-a-quarter to one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we are talking about finishing this witness on Thursday, I do believe we can do that. I have not consulted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the whole of the Defence; that means all Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, Judge, I haven't discussed that with my colleagues. I do believe that it is doable to finish by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see Mr. Kay nodding, although cautiously, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We await to hear further evidence, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We don't know what's going to be said by the witness. It's viva voce and so that goes into the scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Being third has its advantages and disadvantages. And in this case, we will talk among ourselves, and I'm hopeful that we can get done by Thursday depending on how things go obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As matters stand to this moment, then the Chamber, for scheduling purposes, will continue to think in terms of finishing the witness cross-examination by Thursday. Then, of course, there is still a question of how many questions the Bench would still have and how much time would be needed in re-examination. But I invite all parties to do their utmost best to see whether we do not have to recall the witness at a later stage because I do understand that he's available up to and including Thursday but not on Friday anymore. Mr. Tieger, is that well understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will double -- that is my current understanding but I will check on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also perhaps check how flexible that is. Usually questions of the Bench do not take that much time, but in the end they may take time during the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know Mr. Misetic wanted to say something. But just by way of clarification, and I don't want to take any more time than necessary, I may conclude the examination not taking the full session. I wasn't intending to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for speaking out of turn and ask your permission to address one administrative matter, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We received an e-mail this morning from the registrar that there is an issue with respect to courtroom 2 tomorrow and the number of staff that can be present in the courtroom for it. That may be an issue for us because we have several people working on this witness who we would need in court to assist us during the cross-examination. So if the Court could keep that in mind and perhaps consider during the break how we resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a practical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Thursday is courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a look at it and then see with the assistance of the registry how we can resolve the matter. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber is considering solutions for Thursday and we are exploring options and see how it works and we'll certainly find a solution one way or the other. Then Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, do you recall when the shelling ceased, if it did, on the 4th of August, 1995 in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of my recollection, the shelling almost ceased by nightfall; but to the best of my recollection, there was still the occasional explosion at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of what was happening with the civilian population in Knin either during the course of the day or during the evening of August 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: During the main body of the day from 6.45 until the evening, I was not personally out and about in the town of Knin. So my information is based on reports from others who were -- who were out and about and reporting back to either the operations centre or myself, as the Chief of Staff, in terms of trying to ensure that all our people had been recalled. You could see just beside Sector South headquarters is one of the main routes from the zone of separation into Knin; and starting in the afternoon, an almost endless stream of vehicles carrying males dressed in fatigues, some not, were coming into Knin, and everywhere there were reports of civilians leaving starting in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see vehicles coming into and/or leaving Knin in the latter part of the day on August 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: More towards evening and dark fall, sir. When I went -- popped up to see the Serbian liaison officer, who was actually not there when I arrived, at what I call the RSK headquarters, there was still significant numbers of people on the road starting -- continuing the move out; and as well, you could see from the helipad an almost endless string of lights of vehicles climbing the road on the other side of Knin up into the mountains to the north and west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles are we -- did you observe? What kind of vehicles are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: At close range, right by Sector South headquarters, there was a wide range of vehicles, mainly trucks carrying people. We call them putt-putt tractors. Those are essentially large farm implements with a wooden cargo carrying compartment on the back, carrying people. The occasional tank would grind its way back, very rare, covered in soldiers, but not many; and also people on foot walking by the headquarters heading down towards Knin. The road that I could see from -- when it got truly dark that you could see from the helipad, it was too far away to discern the types of vehicles that were actually leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said these tractors with wooden compartment on the back carrying people, what kind of people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It varied, sir. At times, there would be soldiers - this was towards nightfall - soldiers on the back of these cargo pallets. At other times, soldiers mixed in with the women and children, the elderly, so the whole gamut.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were these people coming into Knin and staying there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No. They were coming into Knin to, what we later found out, was to pick up their families or their possessions and to escape via that road that I referred to earlier to the north and west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the stream of vehicles you talked about, were they, therefore, passing through Knin on their way elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I -- once they disappeared from view, I have no knowledge of whether or not the same vehicles exited, but it is a logical assumption that they would not abandon a vehicle considering gasoline was in such short supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, before the next morning, did UNCRO Sector South receive information concerning the possibility or anticipation of further shelling the next day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This information originated from the OPs centre. I believe UNCRO headquarters had relayed such to Sector South headquarters. I can't recall the exact time that we were made aware that essentially the day's activities of the 4th would be repeated on the 5th, but it was common knowledge certainly by midnight or so on the 4th that we could expect another intense barrage at 5.00 on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: With true military precision, at 5.00 on the 5th, there was another intense barrage which replicated in almost every fashion exactly the circumstances the 4th; in other words, between 5.00 and roughly 7.00, intense barrage which appeared to be all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after 7.00?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: After 7.00, the conditions of the 4th were replicated. The barrage diminished markedly, but it was still of a medium intensity and remained such until around 10.30 or 11.00. The same target grid procedure that I referred to in my earlier testimony was replicated from about 7.00 until 10.30 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe the shelling of the 5th; and, if so, was it from the same or different places than you had observed on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It was essentially the same places that I had observed on the 4th, with the exception that I did not get up to the helipad from about -- I did not get up to the helipad at all on the morning of the 5th. By the time I got up to the helipad on the 5th, the shelling had ceased. It was later that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you leave the Sector South headquarters compound on the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: We had been asked by a Serbian physician to assist in the evacuation of approximately 30 to 40 critical patients at the Knin hospital, and I had volunteered to assemble a team of initially six vehicles to proceed to the hospital to assist in that evacuation. We first became aware of this request around 7.00, 7.30 in the morning, and we left the compound about an hour and a half later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of that trip from the Sector South headquarters to the hospital and back, can you tell the Court what, if anything, you saw or experienced?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The journey was -- took approximately 15 to 20 minutes. We started with six vehicles. We were -- initially, my vehicle was going to lead, but at some point the Serbian ambulance cut in front, I think during one of the moments of shell fire. There were two significant periods of shell fire en route. One was in the area of the train yards before you got to the main traffic circle, quite close to the vehicles, to the extent that they were rocked by the blast. The second, which was in the area of -- or prior to the north Dalmatian corps headquarters, after the traffic circle. En route to the town, the town appeared to be, from what I could see, essentially deserted. There were dead along the route, numbering somewhere in the order of 15 to 20 scattered hither and yon, along that main route, occasionally up the side street. There was an enormous debris field along that route of baggage and suit cases and even furniture until we got to the turn-off which left Knin to the north and west, at which point the route became relatively clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing dead along the route to the hospital. Did you see any bodies or injured persons upon arrival at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: On arrival at the hospital, there were large quantities of dead, men, women, and children, stacked in the hospital corridors in a pile. A makeshift room on the back rear floor was being used as a morgue. There was no power, and the medical staff had departed with the exception of one male nurse who had obviously stayed there while the Serbian physician came and got us. There were approximately 30 to 40 patients of which 25 or so were in absolutely critical condition, a mix of the elderly women, occasional fighting-age male, and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we ask the witness "large quantities of dead, men, women, and children, stacked in the hospital ..." What do I have to understand approximately by large quantities? Where you are saying "30 to 40 patients, 25 in absolutely critical condition," what about the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, it's very difficult to estimate. I would say the number was no lower than 30 and probably no higher than 50 or 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the tens of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While at the hospital on the morning of the 5th, did you see signs of shell damage or observe any shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did not observe any signs of shell damage when we pulled up to the hospital, though I was not looking that closely. While we were checking the rooms, a shell landed close enough to punch out several of the windows. But the shell did not hit the hospital, some of the splinters did. I think it was localised. I do not recall any other damage, apart from those windows, those few windows being knocked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, is it your view that there was an effort to destroy the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir. I would argue the reverse. I think the Croatian authorities or the Croatian Army took extraordinary pains not to engage the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While at the hospital, did you see any military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was a tank at about 400 metres, and this is when we left which was around 10.00 or 10.30. Probably closer to 10.30, a tank about 400 -- approximately 400 metres to the north and east. And to be honest, the only reason we noticed it, because we were very busy trying to load the patients into the armoured vehicles, is that it fired into Knin, one round.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you able to tell from what forces or with what forces that tank was -- that's an awkwardly phrased question. Can you tell whether that was a Serbian tank or a Croatian tank or any other kind of tank?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About what time did you return from the hospital, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Approximately 11.00, but it's a very approximate time frame, and we then unloaded the patients and I had to help deal with the issue of the displaced persons and creating space for the patients to be treated at the Czech hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you indicated yesterday that the shelling ceased around the time that -- on August 5th, around the time that the Croatian army entered Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm a bit puzzled by the "yesterday" reference. "I believe you indicated yesterday ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The previous session. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask that in a different way for clarification. Do you recall about when the Croatian army entered Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I believe it was at approximately 11.00, but they first entered Knin - I now know, I did not know at the time - from the north. So the lead elements, we think, of the Croatian army were in Knin at around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry to jump and a bit, but I realise looking at the transcript that there's one question in connection with the hospital that I didn't ask you. You indicated you saw the tank about 400 metres from the hospital fire one round into Knin. Did you see any artillery fire or other fire directed at the tank?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I did not. And there were rounds landing when we arrived at the hospital. There were artillery rounds landing 400, 500, 600 metres from the hospital to the north and the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, your question included that one shell was fired. I do not see that in 42, 18 where the witness said "The only reason we noticed it, because we were very busy trying to load the patients into the armoured vehicles, is that it fired ..." -- I'm sorry. I didn't read it carefully. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, after the Croatian army forces entered Knin, did UNCRO personnel monitor what was happening in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: As the Croatian forces entered Knin, General Forand had decided to take a column of vehicles into town, and he encountered the lead elements of the Croatian army coming south while he was going north and I believe that time was at approximately 11.30. General Forand and his party were then escorted by the Croatian army back to the compound. Prior to him arriving back at the compound at around 11.15ish, though these times are very approximate, the Croatian army had come up to the front gates of the Sector South compound and refused to allow us out. So we could not monitor what was taking place downtown, with that brief period of exception for when General Forand was actually intermixed with the lead elements of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that refusal enforced in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: We tested it. I led a small team out to the crossroads about 150 metres to the left after ignoring the Croatian infantry who were at our front gate. We were then essentially herded back to the Sector South compound by a few tanks, and a tank parked itself at our front gate thereby not allowing egress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that tank or any other military force remain at the compound to prevent UNCRO personnel from leaving the compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the -- no, that's the problem with asking a compound question. Let's focus on the tank for the moment. Where was the tank placed? How was it placed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The tank was placed with its front right up against the gate with the muzzle poking through the gate aimed directly into the compound. It was surrounded or was flanked on both sides by significant numbers of what I assumed to be Croatian infantry; and within 15 to 20 minutes of the block being put in place, a Croatian colonel, I believe, showed up, and we exchanged points of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear on the exchange of points of view, did you demand on behalf of UNCRO that UNCRO personnel be permitted to leave the compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you explain for what purpose UNCRO wanted to leave the compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was that purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: To ensure that the laws of war were being respected, to ensure that no humanitarian violations were being perpetrated, to allow us access and visibility as per the United Nations Security Council resolutions which granted us such, and I also mentioned that we were willing to accept the responsibility and risk in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you recall, what response did you receive to the demand to leave the compound?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Endless repetitions of no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did -- for how long did the tank remain there and how long was UNCRO personnel prevented from leaving the camp?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: We were prevented from leaving the camp up until the 9th of August, where I believe I was one of the first outside of the camp. There had been other minor exceptions, and I was escorted by a Captain of Marine Lukovic from Sector South headquarters out of the area of operations to take up my new duties of Chief of Staff UNCRO. The tank remained in place for several hours. I cannot recall when it left. I was not there when it was withdrawn. By then we had received orders from UNCRO telling us that we were to stay in the camp until a variety of higher-level discussions were conducted between UNPF, UNCRO, and the various authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Although unable to leave the compound, were you able to hear anything that was happening outside the compound during the period of time you were prevented from leaving?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.
