There were occasional flurries of shots, occasional grenade detonation; a modest, very few number of buildings were in flames; and much mechanised noise of tanks grinding by our headquarters to the north on that road; and Croatian forces streaming into the town from that road just outside Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated on a couple of occasions that you assumed your duties as Chief of Staff UNCRO in Zagreb on the 9th. Shortly after arriving in Zagreb, did you file a report about what had happened on August 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, can the registrar call up 65 ter number 4067, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, looking at 4067, is this the report you filed on August 12th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be marked and tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My understanding, Judge, is that the witness statements were not being put in. It was just viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a contemporaneous report -- roughly contemporaneous report immediately after the events filed by this witness to UNCRO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it comes very close to a 92 ter, to say the least, even if it's contemporaneous. Perhaps, Mr. Kehoe, I will first give you an opportunity what, apart from the formal aspect of that it would be a viva voce testimony, apart from that, whether you would have any objections on the basis of the content as well, of course which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The content speaks for itself. Certainly, I do have cross-examination on the content of the document. But I was just moving under the assumption that we were just doing -- we were moving under the assumption that it was not going to be a 92 ter witness and that this was just going to be a viva voce witness. That's why I'm somewhat surprised that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. What is the format side of it and the substance of the -- I mean, the Chamber has seen this report. It was delivered to the staff. I'm always a bit in doubt as to how to approach these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was also included on the exhibit list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, anything else on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Judge. It's -- obviously, I will cross on this matter. The issue I have is frankly one of admissibility at this point given that I thought we were moving as viva voce and not 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to put this statement or report to the witness in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not be very practical, then, to have if in evidence? I mean, Mr. Tieger might even leave it to you to tender it if -- I'm just wondering what, of course for Mr. Tieger, what does it add exactly, apart from, let's say, arithmetics which are not always easy for me to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, the significance, at least in part, is the timing of the submission of this document. Going more broadly to the point, the Court made -- I think this information -- it doesn't really serve any practical purpose not to have this document admitted. So I wasn't trying to circumvent any procedure, just trying to get to the issues involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what the Chamber could learn from this is what the witness testified today that -- that approximately the same what he had in mind already at that time when considering the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was reminded by my colleague, Mr. Cayley, that I do believe that the Prosecutor served us that on us as a statement of the witness, to the extent that plays into the 92 ter matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always understood 92 ter to primarily deal with statements that were given for the purposes of proceedings before this Tribunal, and not every single statement that was given or taken contemporaneously. But these are different types of statements. If you go to a witness and ask him specific questions, of course then the question -- this is 12th of August, which is rather putting on paper, from what I understand, what the witness had observed at the time, rather than to being interviewed by some agency; although, I must admit that on the basis of what I've read from it, violations of the law were certainly in the back of the mind of the witness. That goes without saying. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber admits the document into evidence on the assumption that other counsel has not jumped up and have no objections in addition to what Mr. Kehoe already told us. Yes. Mr. Registrar that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P84, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. P84 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, you've already had an opportunity to discuss the protest letter by General Forand in which attacks on civilians are alleged; and, as just noted, you, yourself prepared a report upon arrival at UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb in which you describe the events and asserted that Croatian authorities either indiscriminately or deliberately fired on civilian residential areas. I'd like you then, please, to explain to the Court what it was that you observed that reflected either the deliberate targeting of civilians or indiscriminate shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the problem. He's now using this particular report to bootstrap his individual testimony. Now, if the witness is going to testify as to what the witness heard or observed with regard to this, that's fine. But, I mean, now bootstrapping this with this document, this is clearly what he's, you know, an elaboration of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be just the way in which the question is put. I -- I understand that where, of course, the Chamber has seen these documents, where quite a lot of conclusions are drawn; and as it was set out in the decision the Chamber gave earlier this morning, not in the presence of this witness, but certainly relevant for the present interrogation. Mr. Leslie, you come to all kinds of conclusion, conclusions on matters where it's reserved for the Chamber to draw conclusions. At the same time, of course you have looked and observed matters, as becomes clear from this first report, within the back of your mind and as you said was also the task, your task to see whether any violations of the laws, and I take it and the customs of war, were committed or any other international crimes. Now, conclusions, as I said before, are there for the Chamber to draw. At the same time, of course it -- the legal framework, with which you apparently are familiar, may have been of guidance to you when you made your observations at the time. For example, just to give an example, that a doctor might look primarily at the injuries of a person; whereas, a lawyer might perhaps first look at whether someone is in civilian or in military clothes. That's just the difference of approach. Now, what I assume Mr. Tieger is asking you is whether you could share with us your observations in light of what apparently was on your mind as a question; that is, are any crimes committed? So, therefore, we are not seeking your conclusions primarily; but if you, for example, say: I saw a ratio of 99.9 civilians to be hit and 0.1 soldiers, that might be relevant observation for drawing conclusions. Now, I think Mr. Tieger is at this moment trying to find out what you observed factually, and perhaps he will lead you in some more detail, rather than to tell us what your conclusions were. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court is correct. I'd like to focus on what you observed in light of your experience with artillery and your understanding of weapons systems that led you to the conclusions you made. So, first of all, with respect to the initial barrage that took place on August 4th, what was it about that initial barrage, if anything, that led to the conclusions you drew in the August 12th report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The initial barrage on the 4th of August from approximately 5.00 to approximately 7.00 in the morning did not have any concentration of fire and no discernible pattern that corresponded to any obvious point of aim of military value. The fire was, to put it in layman's terms, all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And although that may seem obvious, what's the significance of that with respect to the -- either the conclusion that the shelling of civilian areas was deliberate or was indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: If the fire was all over the place and was not concentrated or appeared to be directed towards any specific point, then, as a gunner, there's a variety of conclusions one could reach. One is that it's either indiscriminate in which the centre of mass of Knin is a free fire zone in and amongst the civilian structures and residences, or it is a deliberate attempt to distribute the fire such that the same effect occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated, during the course of your discussion, about events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just put one question to the witness, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that your answers are based at this moment on the assumption that military targets were not all over the place, to use the same terminology, because then you could say: I'm targeting deliberately all the military targets that were all over the place. That's it. I'm just thinking in terms of logic, and I'm trying to follow your logic at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I think your logic is impeccable. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Although, I wasn't seeking that kind of compliments; nevertheless, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, you also indicated that during the course of the shelling that took place on August 4th and August 5th, you observed corrected fire or target group procedures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would that indicate that there was -- would that reflect, based on your observations and your experience, that was an effort to hit particular targets?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, where did you see those target group procedures or corrected fire? Where was it directed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: In the main, from the vantage points which I enjoyed which were either the balcony or perhaps more specifically the region of the helipad, the vast majority of the target grid procedure centre of mass impact were in and amongst residential structures. There were some exceptions to this, and I do not know if you wish me to go into the detail at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. What were the exceptions to this, do you wish to let us know?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The exceptions to this were - and this is not an exhaustive list because I would like to refer to my notes to provide such - the air defence battery which was located 400 to 600 metres to the south and east of Sector South headquarters, which was -- which was well and truly covered by fire by Croatian artillery systems; the south-east portion of the train yards; and what was known as the factory complex, the roof of which you could see from the helipad. Those were the only three that immediately spring to mind that I could see from where I was in Sector South helipad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, returning back to a question posed earlier - a couple of questions posed earlier, in fact - with respect to the initial barrage on both days in roughly of first couple of hours of the morning. Could the fire that you observed have been directed toward particular military targets to the extent that such targets might exist; that is, assuming that the entire town was not a military target, was the nature of the shelling that took place during the initial barrages such that it could have been directed toward particular targets or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: To be clear, sir, from the period of roughly 5.00 to 6.00, I did not observe the artillery fire, so I can give you no visual confirmation as to that sequence of events. When I saw it at 6.00 and subsequent to that, the answer to your question is no. It was distributed across the entire town and there was no concentration of fire, which even though you couldn't see the exact point of impact of these shells, you could certainly throughout the majority of town see the plumes, the dust clouds, and the smoke from the impacts which would break the roof line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you a question about military targets, if I may. First of all, what is a legitimate military target, in general?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: A legitimate military target is one which is deemed by an attacking commander to have a significant military value, one in which its neutralisation or destruction will provide a significant advantage to the attacking force, and one which has military utility which is current. There are other criteria, but I would have to refer to notes to get more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once a legitimate military target, to use that parlance, is identified, does that mean that it can then be shelled?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, most absolutely not. Identifying a legitimate military target is merely the first step in a process. The second step is determining its current military relevance, it's utility, the possibility of collateral damage to innocent lives or civilian structure, the military utility of prosecuting that target commensurate with the rules of law, what type of weapon system you have to engage that target to avoid the potential of collateral damage, and then finally, of course, the gut check to see whether or not you think it's the right thing to do considering all the factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the residential areas to which you saw corrected fire being directed. What if, for example, a significant military figure lived in one of the apartment buildings located within that residential area, would that mean that the corrected fire you saw being directed into the residential neighbourhood, therefore, be permissible and would that render your conclusions drawn in the August 12th statement -- report wrong?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, I will offer you my opinion based on a variety of years of experience in these matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's offering his opinion; he's not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as I said before and as is found in the Chamber's decision, that sometimes it's not easy to distinguish, especially when you have professionals testifying. Mr. Tieger, what I notice at this moment is the following: That you started asking the witness about what he considers to be a military target, a legitimate military target. I had already some doubts at this moment, but at the same time, I thought it might be good to know whether this witness understands this, to be whether that's correct or not. And then what was done is that we actually moved from what a legitimate military target is into the process of decision-making on whether or not to attack a certain target. For example, the type of weaponry used is not -- is, of course, a consideration which may be of importance; at the same time, it does not change the target as a legitimate military target automatically. Let's try to focus at this moment, first of all, on facts, because your question was of a high hypothetical nature, at least you have chosen to make it a hypothetical question. I could imagine that a similar question in a less hypothetical way would be put to the witness, but let's try not to lose ourselves in hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, what kind of weapons systems did you see being directed toward the residential neighborhoods where you saw corrected fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I never saw the point of origin of the shell fire. The explosions were commensurate with fire from a variety of medium and heavier calibre indirect fire artillery systems which are, by definition, at least with the technology available to the Croatian army at that time, area weapons systems, not pinpoint strike systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can those weapons systems distinguish between particular military targets, between a particular building which might have a military value sufficient to render it a legitimate military target and the civilian structures that surround it or are adjacent to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Simplistically, no. The actual zone in which an artillery shell will land --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge. This is clearly expert testimony. We are getting into an area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tend to agree. Mr. Tieger, what we are talking about at this moment, you, in your question, "Can those weapons systems distinguish between particular military targets, between a building which might have a military value sufficient to render it a legitimate military target ..." Now, that's again kind of a theoretical question because it all depends, isn't it, on the size of the premises? I can imagine single buildings. I am aware of the existence of Ministries of Defence in this world, which may be clearly separated from all the surroundings and may have a huge surface. So, therefore, I think that these type of questions do not assist the Chamber very much. Of course, you could ask, and that's a very simple question: What is the range of area for a certain type of weaponry? How precise is it? Then whether that's expertise or whether that's something an experienced professional could tell this Court on the basis of his experience is still to be seen. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would ask for -- and that's why if there is going to be some discussion about this, the witness, in order to render any kind of view on that, has got to know the weapons system because every weapons system has a different margin of error. And if he doesn't know the weapons system and doesn't know the range --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let's ask him what he knows about the range, what he knows about it. I mean, I think I've been quite clear that I agree with you that we could not just put questions, and let me just find exactly where we started again. Yes. The question was about "those weapons systems." So, therefore, we limit ourselves to the weapons systems the witness testified about, and then we could ask him whether he knows any further details; and whether within this type of weapons systems, whether the variation and precision is such, that this is, I think, knowledge an experienced professional could have. And if the witness doesn't have that knowledge, he'll tell us. Now, to what extent that is just at or beyond the border of factual testimony or expertise, we can consider that. But for the time being, Mr. Tieger, you are invited to focus on these kind of questions which avoid some of the legitimate concerns of Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that and will do so. However, if I'm not arguing with the Court's ruling, I just wasn't given an opportunity, I think, to clarify one aspect of that, and that's the following: I think witnesses, recipient witnesses with the right backgrounds, should be in a position to assist the Court by advising the Court what they observed and what conclusions they were able to draw from that. I had pointed to -- it may have appeared to have been a broadly-framed question. I had attempted to focus it on his observations of the particular neighborhoods on the 4th and 5th where he observed corrected fire. So that was a particular context related to -- rather than a broad one that might have been embraced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- a series of speculative responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still, then, that's part of the story, Mr. Tieger; that is to say, corrected or adjusted fire. At the same time, it might make a difference from what weaponry system these shells were fired. Perhaps you should just explore whether it's known; and if it's not known, whether this still allows for any conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, you've obviously heard a good deal of the discussion and part of the interest is in knowing, to the extent you were aware, what weapons systems were used on Knin on the 4th and 5th of August and their precision or lack of precision.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The weapons systems that -- first of all, my knowledge of the weapons systems used comes from many years of experience in listening to shells detonate. The vast majority of shells which I heard detonate were of medium calibre. So, as I mentioned earlier, I did not see the guns that fired these shells. They were out of visual range and remained so. On my times watching the Croatian army advance into and through Knin, a variety of 122-millimetre Howitzers and some D33 guns were towed right past our sector headquarters. So I can try and connect the dots in my mind. Plus, the lists of weapons systems which were currently in the Croatian inventory is readily well-known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not to us, Judge, and obviously not to Mr. Munkelien either, the witness that was here the other day either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is comment, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I suggest that we strike that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, could you elicit from the witness what he apparently knows and what we might not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Leslie, the Court would like to know what weapons systems you understand were -- what weapons systems were available, but I think more to the point, what weapons systems you understand were used on the 4th and 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, excuse me. I mean, use of the verb "understand." I mean, we're talking about was what he knows was used, not a speculation as to using the verb "understand." It's what he knows were used. I think that's the issue that we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Knowledge is often based on understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it's how he listened to the question and carefully listen to the answer which interests us, perhaps even more than exactly the way in which it was phrased. Of course, if I understand something to be A or B, then I have -- I can explain the reasons why I understand this to be A or B; and in an explanation of those reasons, usually you find the facts the Chamber is interested in. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me start back toward the beginning. What weapons systems, that you were you aware of, did you know that the Croatian military had available? Was the UN told about that? Did you explore it in other ways?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The weapons systems that we told were available to the Croatian army, and which I physically saw in my many interactions along the zone of separation on both the Croatian and Serbian side, were medium-weight mortars of approximately 82 millimetres in diameter, 122-millimetre guns, 130-millimetre guns, 152-millimetre guns, and a variety of rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the witness was referring to both sides. That might need some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In -- General Leslie, your answer referred to "both." So if there are any weapons systems that were exclusive to one side or the other, you'll need to assist the Court, because, at the moment, the Court is interested in knowing who you know about the weapons systems that the Croatian side had.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: All of those, sir, are based on my knowledge of or understanding of what the Croatian side had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you refer to a variety of rockets launchers, are those multiple-barrel rocket launchers or MBRLs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So working backwards on the kinds of weapons that you were discussing, what is the variation and precision and, indeed, what is the general purpose of MBRLs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Multiple-barrel rocket launchers are an area suppression weapon system whose individual rocket accuracy is not high; and so the tactical utility of them comes by massing your five and covering an area which, for planning purposes for all rocket launchers in this broad range, is a block of ground roughly 400 metres left and right from the line between the rocket launcher and the target and 200 to 300 metres in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And you referred earlier in your testimony to area weapons. What about the other weapons systems that you listed in your answer a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The relatively unsophisticated nature of the indirect fire systems that I referred to more often than not indicated that they would have an accuracy which is dependent on range, dependent on the charge used; but in terms of a generality, if you got it within 400 metres of your opening point of aim, you would then visually correct that fire on to your target. So landing within a 400 metre radius of your target with your first shot would be considered within acceptable norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the legitimate military targets which you identified in Knin on August 4th, did you see fire that was -- that indicated an effort to take out those military targets exclusively?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I saw some of those targets being engaged with target grid procedure which, in some cases, indicated that it was an exclusive attempt to hit only those targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With that particular corrected fire procedure?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what about in the context of the overall shelling that you observed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The best descriptor between the periods 5.00 and 7.00 in the morning on the 4th and 5th of August was the fire was all over the place, and there was no apparent target grid procedure that I could discern, and that in the periods on both days from 7.00 until when the fire stopped, the target grid procedure, some of which was fired at some of the targets which I believed to be legitimate military targets, the vast majority which was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have a few questions to better understand your testimony, but, first, Judge Gwaunza has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Mr. Leslie, you said in answer to a question from Mr. Tieger that on the night of the 4th, there were occasional explosions heard. Was there any way of saying whether those explosions were targeted at any specific places or rather whether there were any specific targets?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, ma'am, there was not. We were not equipped with night observations devices, and the detonations were outside of my visual view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you mentioned collecting critically injured people from the hospital and taking them to the UN camp. Is that the same camp that was the then barricaded by the tank that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: So would you say the injured that were there inside the camp were affected in any way by that activity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I would not. I would say that they had access to reasonable care from the Czech medical company, which provided excellent support to those critical injured personnel. In all fairness, the level of facilities available to the Czechs was what we categorise as a role 2, which means they can do immediate life-saving surgery but not anything more complicated than that. I'm not sufficiently versed in medical -- the arts of medicine to give you a more coherent answer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following: You have answered many questions about shelling of Knin city, shell impact, and it was never specifically asked whether you were aware or whether you observed anything that allowed you to conclude by what party the shells were fired.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, I never saw the point of origin of any of the indirect fire systems that engaged Knin between the 4th and 5th of August. So I have been operating on the assumption, as have many others, that the fire originated from the attacking Croatian army. But that is an assumption because we did not -- we saw them land, but I never, in my time there, saw the Croatian artillery actually fire at Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you observe anything that would run counter to the assumption you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question would be: You described that you saw dead people when you were on the road to the hospital. Did you observe anything which would give a clue to whether their status was civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain what you observed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: There were - it was long ago - but I believe that there were a few dead children -- well, there were certainly some, very young. There were women dressed in skirts. There were fighting-aged males as well, dressed with the sort of unique collection of clothing that the Serbian militia wore at that time. There were a few elderly. Most of the dead, though, were essentially shapeless bundles of rags with the occasional limb protruding or other unpleasantness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand were your answer that you're not able to give any more precise proportions of the categories you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you told us about soldiers on the wooden cargo pallets behind the tractors. You said that you saw, together with women and elderly people, you saw also soldiers. Could you be more precise as what soldiers of what armed forces, if you are able to make any distinction in that respect? Could you tell us a bit more about these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. Starting in the afternoon of the 4th, the soldiers were Serbian soldiers and it started slowly, this column of vehicles. But within a couple of hours, it was very constant and steady where you'd have trucks carrying two or three soldiers, five or six women and children; followed by a putt-putt, which is this tractor pulling this wooden cargo flat rack, that might have all soldiers; followed by a normal tractor pulling a hay wagon that would have all women and children. So it was truly a chaotic melange of people driving by Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Before an opportunity will be given to Defence counsel to cross-examine you, we'll first have a break as requested. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that you arranged that you would be the one to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Leslie, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. General, you mentioned during your direct examination that you had taken a trip out, I believe you said, approximately 6.00 a.m. on the 4th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I ask if the clerk can bring up 65 ter 4769.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for this, if the pacing seems a bit slow, I am attempting to allow the translators to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just blow up the bottom half of that or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, as you see on the map here, it is an overhead of Knin, and as I'm sure you can observe on the right-hand side of that photograph is the UN facility. With the assistance of the usher, could you please draw on that map and tell us the route you took when you left for the first time on the 6th -- excuse me, on the 4th of August, 1995, at 6.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can't be precise as to the exact time. I said approximately 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, you marked in blue the route coming back down and coming down the main street and then returning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how long a period of time was this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Twelve, ten, fifteen-ish minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you accompanied with others?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was. It was a Jordanian vehicle with a Jordanian driver and a Jordanian crew commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know who those Jordanians were, their names?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted for us that you went to pick up or attempted to pick up some UN CIVPOL people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was involved in that. It wasn't me who was trying to pick them up. I was there. It was the Jordanian vehicle that was actually going to go off and do that organized by the CIVPOL, I believe, confused mix of vehicles at the front gate; and they wanted someone who knew where this approximate location was, and I was available to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this location is how far away from the base?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Probably as the route flies, 1.000-odd metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your testimony is that the people that were in this Jordanian APC didn't know where this location was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct, at least they gave every indication they didn't know where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who were you supposed to pick up at this location?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: There was some UN CIVPOL at a specific address. We did not pick up the UN CIVPOL, but there were three civilian employees that we - I didn't see because I was in the back of the vehicle - the Jordanian person, who was crew commanding it, stopped, lowered the ramp, picked them up, and we came back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were the CIVPOL --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, who were the CIVPOL people who you were supposed to be picking up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It was an address. There was a couple of folk there. I cannot recall the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the people that you actually did pick up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Three civilian employees, and I'm sorry it's been so long, I do not recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have this marked as an exhibit and moved into evidence at this time. This map itself, Your Honour, is independently is P62; however, this, I believe, would be a D exhibit given it has the witness's markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I take it no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D112, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D112 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, what was the address, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't, nor can I recall the address for which I lived for five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, let us turn to yet another version of this particular 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, if we could bring up a fresh version of 65 ter 4769.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at 4769 anew, sir, you said you took another trip later on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where is that location, sir? Could you take us again with the marker and mark the route that you took.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, again, you've marked, in blue, going to the same road yet a little bit further, and it appears to be a turn around in and around -- just north of where it says "parliament"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, where did you go, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Went to meet with a Serbian liaison officer who called my office and wanted to talk about some details on Serbian -- sorry, displaced persons who were in our compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was that individual's name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: If you'll permit me to look at my notes, I will be able to give you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Feel free, sir. And what are you looking at, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at a statement that I provided to investigators from this Court in 1997 but were actually signed by me in 1999. The officer named, I believe, was Captain Karlopac [phoen]. That's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain Karlopac. Now, that particular statement that you have in 1997 -- now, by the way, on this particular trip that you went to, I believe you said it was sometime in the late afternoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It was evening and night; it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give me an approximate time frame?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I went in a Jordanian armoured personnel carrier accompanied by a Jordanian captain with the name of Mohammed who was my military assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall what his last name is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: His last name is Mohammed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: His last name is Mohammed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And other than that trip, were those the only trips you took on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: You mean trips in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Trips in a vehicle into Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how about trips outside a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: There was a couple of brief forays to the front gate and beyond as part of the endless tour, the cycle of activity that I would engage in throughout the day on the 4th, checking on the front gate, seeing how the retrieval plan was going for the UN staffers and a variety of military officers, but I didn't progress any distance at all from the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just going back before we go into the gate situation. With regard that the two of you went in with vehicles, and I think you described them as mounted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the two vehicles that were mounted, in both of those were you back in the APC?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: In both of the cases, I was back in the APC, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during that period of time, you did not observe any shelling while you were in the back of that APC, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The hatch, the top hatch was open. I could certainly hear the shell fire. I did not see any detonations in close proximity to the vehicles, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you -- I apologise. Just waiting while everyone catches up, General. So when you told the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997, and then subsequently signed the document in 1999, that you had personally witnessed shell fire on three occasions during your trips through Knin during the shell fire, that wasn't true; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Personally witnessed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, what does "personally witnessed" mean? If I heard shell fire in close proximity, the detonation of a shell in close proximity of to a vehicle or in relative proximity to a vehicle, I would say that's me witnessing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, when you told the Office of the Prosecutor, and you can review your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A pause, every time, between answer and question; and for you, Mr. Leslie, the same, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, and my apologies to the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, unfortunately, I'm unable to follow the B/C/S translation. I'm usually listening to the French. If there is any problem there, I might switch to B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So General, when you told the Office of the Prosecutor in a statement -- by the way, the statement that you gave in 1997, you dictated that statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: In part. There was also a series of note takers there. You will forgive me, but I can't remember the name of the investigator. The statement then was then taken away and returned to me two years later at which point I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you read it before you signed it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I probably did not read it carefully enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, certainly, sir, your interview in 1997 was closer to the events in 1995 than when you ultimately signed it in 1999, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what else could -- isn't this one of these fully superfluous questions. 2000 is later than 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Often, Your Honour, in the spirit of confessions, as my learned colleague, Mr. Cayley said, we are examples of the systems from which we grew up, and that's unfortunately one of the frailties and I will attempt to change that as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have all have to adapt to a new situation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you did say in 1997 that you personally witnessed these on three occasions during trips through Knin during the shell fire; didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, I did. However, as I pointed out in my previous testimony, only rarely did I see a point of detonation. The vast majority of shells which I witnessed were either through oral or the smoke and glass of dust cloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you also explain to the Office of the Prosecutor when you gave that statement that, in fact, you never took three trips through Knin during the shell fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd have to refer to that, but may I say that the testimony I gave in 1995 was taken away and sent back to me. There are some variances and inaccuracies in that testimony, which I'm more than willing to admit to, and certain nuancing and wording that I did not pay enough attention to when I actually signed it two years later. I believe I was thinking at the time that one of those trips, especially the one on the evening of the 4th, that there was almost no shell fire and certainly not along the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you told us today you had two mounted trips out; and in the statement that you gave in 1997, you said that you went out on three occasions. Now I ask you to take a look at P84.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can put that up on the screen. Your Honour, before I do that, if I could tender the map that we have that's on the screen, my colleague Mr. Misetic informs me that I have not done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. May I have a page reference for the reference in the 1997 statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly. It's 00884726.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try first to deal with the -- you first tendered the aerial photograph and the markings, that's the second marked aerial photograph into evidence. Mr. Tieger, if you could express yourself on any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then Mr. Registrar, this would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D113 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, Mr. Tieger, it is the first full paragraph on that page approximately seven lines down, just for reference sake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I have the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know you do, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was just helping my colleague, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is the document that came into evidence previously and just a -- one point of interest on page 1. You noted -- now this was written several days after you took over as the Chief of Staff UNCRO in Zagreb, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, of course, let me move down the page on 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could blow up paragraph 1, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it notes four lines down that, "I arrived in Knin on 1 March 1995, and departed on 7 August 1995"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this extended conversation that you had with, I believe, it was Captain of Marine Lukovic on the 9th of August; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I recall the conversation because the good navy captain was the officer who drove me from Sector South headquarters to the coast; and if I made a mistake on the date, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in fact, you left Knin on the 7th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I would have to refer to further notes, sir, and documentation. I believe so, on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on the second page of this document, if we can turn to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the paragraph 3 on page 2 because the numbering on this document is a bit confusing. There is a number 3 on paragraph one as well, just for the record. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's it. Thank you. Paragraph 3, if we could just blow that up, and it's the paragraph 3 as Judge Orie pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph, General, details your trip to the hospital on the 5th of August, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's move up to paragraph 2, and it begins on the bottom of the first page and carries over to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just look at that one page, Mr. Monkhouse, and then if we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, if we turn our attention to this paragraph, this discusses the events of the 4th of August and chronicles the attempt by individuals within UN Sector South to bring in UN employees, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not anywhere in that paragraph do you discuss the fact that you went out on the 4th of August to assist in the retrieval of personnel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it mentions Mr. Dawes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And also the other person who is the Sector South security officer, and that would be Mr. Dreyer, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Who both deserve great credit for what they did because they were out all the time, as I mention in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But there's no mention of you, is there, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Well, sir, why would I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there any mention of you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I did not write about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go back, General, to another copy of 65 ter 4769. While we're waiting, General, with regard to this first trip that you say you took down to Knin somewhere after 6.00 in the morning, do you have any better time about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any witness that can corroborate that you took that trip; and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Well, I would assume the Jordanian armoured personnel crew. There had to be some folk down at the front gate, even though it was incredibly chaotic, who saw what was going on and some of the sequence of events of activities. There were dozens of vehicles leaving the camp every 15 to 20 minutes being dispatched to go pick up people. Anyway, I await your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, do you have the name of one person that can corroborate that you took that trip?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't, nor do I have the name of one person that readily springs to mind who can corroborate my trip to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go back to 65 ter 4769, and if we can blow up, Mr. Monkhouse, the area down near the compound, it would be the lower half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you mention that, likewise, sometime on the day of the 4th, you also went out to this area near the compound and there was some activity regarding bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Was that on the 4th or on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can retrieve the transcript, General; but if my memory serves me correctly, you testified this morning that this was on the 4th during one of your unmounted trips?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you give me one moment, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The unmounted trips are found at page 80, line 4 -- no. That's the most recent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This would be at 32, 11. And if I can just scroll up a little bit but, just so that I can put this in context. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can start at 32, 1, so we can put this in context, and the question was about the going out on the 4th, and at line 1: "A couple of times mounted; a couple of times dismounted. The mounted were sometime shortly after 6.00 for a very short duration where, in the controlled chaos, that was the front gate."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is correct. The front gate --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, General, let me finish?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just reading the transcript and then we can go to the question. "There were some issues with UN CIVPOL who were not necessarily on the same recall list as the Sector South United Nations civil staff, and there was a demand for somebody who knew where a street was close to the train yard. So I hopped aboard that vehicle. The duration of the trip was about 15 minutes, nothing significant to report. Picked up three people, none of them CIVPOL, and came back. The second trip was at some point during the day. There was some bodies outside to the right, and some people were interested in investigating them and putting them in bags. So I just went outside to put a stop to that." It is that incident that I am referring to, and I'd like you to address in the chart that is -- or the map that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just pause for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did this trip take place on the 4th or on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Drawing, using this particular map that's on the screen, again in the same fashion that we employed previously, could you tell us the route that you took and where these bodies were located?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It is not a long trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, General.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Okay. About there, to the best of my memory. I take no credit for anything that happened. It was soldiers out there trying to put bodies in bags which I thought exposed them to unnecessary risk, so I brought them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And at that particular time, who was with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I believe one of the Canadian captains was, but I'm not entirely sure. I think it might have been Captain Berikoff. You will have to ask him. Sir, it was 12 years ago, one of many, many incidents in a very compressed time frame. So you will forgive me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I assume before you came here today that you read your five statements that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm sure that refreshed you on the facts and circumstances of this, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately, what time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It was sometime in the morning, but, I'm sorry, I can't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can have this, Your Honour, with a D number introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D114 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could have yet another version of 65 ter 4769 put on the screen. Mr. Monkhouse, if we could just take a larger view of that. No, I'm sorry. I meant the other way. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, on the 5th, you noted that you went out to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, approximately, what time was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It was at approximately 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, approximately, what time did this Serbian doctor come to the gate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was not there when he first arrived. I became aware of the issue sometime between 7.00 and 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was fair to say he was there prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, if we could use this map, and if you could take your pen and indicate to us the path that you followed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: [Marks] Well, both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You followed the same road back?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, who was with you on this trip?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: We had the Serbian doctor, whose name I cannot recall; we had two Canadian M-113 armoured personnel carriers; two Jordanian M-113 armoured personnel carriers; and two Czech armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, do you know the name of anyone who was with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes, actually now I do. Sergeant Marcotte, who was the Canadian sergeant, accompanied me on the trip; and for that specific sequence of events, he was awarded the meritorious service medal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And anyone else, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The names of the Canadian soldiers with a bit of research I could certainly provide to you. I do not recall the names of the Jordanian crews who, of course, spoke no English, and of the Czech crews who spoke no English either or very little, or, to be honest, I don't know if they spoke English or not, but I had very little dealings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you were in this particular, I guess, convoy of vehicles, I mean where were you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was in, originally, the lead vehicle, but then the Serbian doctor, very brave, took the lead, so I was in the first vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where were you in this vehicle, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I was standing in the cargo hatch which was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will come back to these when we go through the actual sequence. Let me talk to you just a bit about the actual operation, Operation Storm, that you spoke about this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe there is a technical problem here as we move into this next area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not knowing the character of the problem, I also have no clue as to whether you would perhaps already continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's really a prelude of what we're going into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there was a computer crash for your team. Is there any other area you could perhaps already touch upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge. I mean, one the one is building on the other, so that's unfortunately the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to wait for a while until a technician can identify the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It appears to be restarting, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that the system is restarting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Will we receive any indication of how much time it will still take --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't understand the nature or the problem of the document, but I just wonder if it's possible to use a hard copy in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I wish there were, I mean. Thanks, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're there, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, before we just go to this, and I would like to pull this up. If I could move the item on the screen into evidence, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the itinerary to and from the hospital. No objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D115 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, before we move to this particular item, could you spell Marcotte for me?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: M-A-R-C-O-T-T-E. If you wish, I can have, subject to access to information regulations of my government, contact details available to you by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to play this individual item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is ID 170388, and this is an audio clip from CBC news online. There is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transcripts are given to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "They're not disgruntled former soldiers, but some of the most senior officers in the Canadian army. Major-General Andrew Leslie leaves for Afghanistan next week where he will command Canadian forces. He says he's never believed that the Croatian army planned Operation Storm on its own. Andrew Leslie: 'That had to have been done by people who were really knew what they were doing. Therefore, I can't see where they would have pulled off the expertise to get it done.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us begin to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Judge, that was a CBC audio clip from July the 21st, 2003. Now, General, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was it about Operation Storm that led you to say that they really knew what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, that opinion was shaped over the subsequent years by, not fact, but by a great or a significant amount of conversation amongst military professionals that a certain nation's contracting service, which specialised in military activities, had been instrumental in assisting the Croatian military authorities in planning and executing Operation Storm. I will be the first to admit I have no proof of such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what country are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, that is beyond my remit to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what company were you talking about that assisted the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, to my mind, without substantive proof, it would be slander to mention this company now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well let's change the question a bit and let's explore your comments on CBC, and explain to us what expertise was used during Operation Storm that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Sir, it was an opinion based on a great deal of conversation amongst military professionals. There is a certain body of view that some military contractors were hired to assist the Croatian government with the synchronisation and the coordination of fires, the timing and the tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's explore that. So what you're saying is that Operation Storm was conducted with a high degree of expertise; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I, as a military professional, would agree that certain elements of Operation Storm were conducted with a high degree of expertise. If the aim was to ensure that the local population was cleansed from the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that what you were referring to in that audio clip when you noted that this was conducted with a high degree of expertise and that they really knew what they were doing? Was that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I can't recall what I was actually thinking when I made those comments many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let us talk, if I may, let us talk about the operation itself. You are familiar, are you not, with various aspects of NATO strategy, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can just put a document up on the screen, and that would be -- before I do that, Judge, I've been reminded, once again, that I should move into evidence the audio clip, 1D17-0388.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D116 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I could put up on the screen ID 170100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is one of two pages, General. If we could just look at the first page that just identifies where the next page comes from, so I give you a point of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the NATO Glossary of Terms and Definitions. If we can go to the next page, and if we could just go down on that page, at the bottom. And if we could blow up that centre of gravity item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the centre of gravity in the NATO definition of the centre of gravity: "Characteristics, capabilities, or localities from which a nation, an alliance, a military force, or other grouping derives its freedom of action, physical strength, or will to fight." Are you familiar with that, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is that a definition that has been incorporated into the Canadian military philosophy?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Essentially. There may be minor variances, but they are of no significant difference from the intent of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the idea of the centre of gravity is that if you can neutralise or destroy the enemy's centre of gravity, it will lead to the destruction of his cohesion and his will to fight; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to the Krajina and, specifically, Knin. Now, Knin was the heart of the Krajina Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you knew, sir, that if the Croatian army could capture Knin, they would he essentially decapitate the Krajina Serb effort; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us, at some length, that you have been an artillery officer for much of your career. Are you familiar with the United States air/land battle doctrine?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Air/land 2000 and 2004, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could -- do you basically agree with the principles that is set forth in that air/land battle doctrine?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: That is a very detailed technically complicated document, so I would further subdivide my approval down into specific blocks before I gave such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just -- if we can hone in a little bit and if we can probably cut down, I know that there may be a lot of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could bring up on the page -- excuse me, if I could bring up on the screen ID 170080

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what are we going to do with the previous document? You read all of it, the centre of gravity and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could move those two documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You read all of what you've drawn our attention to, isn't it? You literally read it, so it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's just so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Tieger? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D117 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in air/land battle, General, are you familiar with concept of deep battle or deep operations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: It's intended to deny the enemy freedom action, disrupt his lines of communication and supply, disrupt and separate the first echelon and second echelon forces from the third and the reinforcing groupings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'll try that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Known one was able to follow you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deep operations are designed to disrupt and nullify the enemy's fire power, to disrupt lines of communication and supply, and in certain contexts, to separate the first and second echelons or the second and third echelons from one another, to create and craft the conditions for exploitation by deep strike forces, and the list goes on. This is not an exhaustive analysis of the deep battle that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by way of reference, General, what I have referenced in front of you from the deep operations is page 146 of an expert report filed by the Office of the Prosecutor by a Mr. Theunens. So this has been a document that's been submitted to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just scroll up a bit and if I could just pull it down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could go from that sentence, that's in paragraph little I: "The deep battle is designed to nullify the enemy's fire power, disrupt his command and control, destroy his supplies, and break his morale. In conducting simultaneous attacks in depth, army forces employ long-range intelligence-acquisition and targeting assets, including electronic warfare and joint assets, to track enemy forces, to complicate their operations, and to determine the effects of our strikes in depth." So the concept, here, General is to move the fighting back behind the initial lines of confrontation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: The concept, sir, is to move the fighting as deep as possible, targeting enemy combatants and not civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question -- did you understand my question, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the answer to my question is this -- is the answer to my question to take the battle inside or deeper into the land than the initial confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW LESLIE
utterances.text: And, sir, without meaning to sound argumentative, before I can give you my answer to that, you'll have to define who you're fighting against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you a question about artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Before we start with the artillery, I'm looking at the clock. We have to finish within the next minute or two minutes. Would you like to start with the artillery?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Artillery is a long story, Judge, so, I mean, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to instruct you, Mr. Leslie, not to speak with anyone about your testimony either already given or still to be given. May I take it that it's more or less agreed that trying to find the name of or at least the whereabouts of a certain person is agreed, that the witness, as a result of his testimony today, I think it was an offer by the witness to find some information, which of course would, under normal circumstances, be directly related to your testimony, but just to find that information without further discussing your testimony. I take it that the parties would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is fine with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger as well. Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow, Mr. Leslie, the 23rd of April, in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00 in courtroom I. Mr. Leslie, I would like to add one thing. You earlier apologised for not having a clear memory of events that took place quite a while ago. There is no need to apologise for that. The only thing we expect you to do is to answer the questions to the best of your abilities; and if you have no recollection, there is no need to apologise. It's just accepted, and you are invited to tell us if you don't remember. So, even if Mr. Kehoe immediately after that referred to you refreshing your memory, nothing wrong with that. If what you saw the last couple of days refreshes your memory, fine. If it doesn't refresh your memory, you should not rely, unless you specifically tell us, on anything you have read over the past few days which has not come back to your memory. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of April, 2008 at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.
